items.question: What does the Kubernetes documentation say about Namespaces of Services?
items.ideal_answer:
A DNS query may return different results based on the namespace of the Pod making
it. DNS queries that don't specify a namespace are limited to the Pod's
namespace. Access Services in other namespaces by specifying it in the DNS query. For example, consider a Pod in a `test` namespace.

### What happened?

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/windows-networking/#limitations states the following as one of the things _not_ supported:
> More than 64 backend pods (or unique destination addresses) for a single Service

The original trigger for this documentation is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/98680 apparently, which led to https://github.com/microsoft/Windows-Containers/issues/93. Comments in the latter issue say that the issue has been fixed with the limit increased to 1024. By now (3 years later), I believe the limitation has been fixed in Windows Server in both 2019 and 2022.

items.question: What does the Kubernetes documentation say about Services in Kubernetes?
items.ideal_answer:
The Service API, part of Kubernetes, is an abstraction to help you expose groups of
Pods over a network. Each Service object defines a logical set of endpoints (usually
these endpoints are Pods) along with a policy about how to make those pods accessible.

items.question: What problem was reported in issue #128162: Pod admission can fail due to webhooks + context deadline ex...?
items.ideal_answer:
Pod admission failed with the error "Timeout: request did not complete within requested timeout - context deadline exceeded"

This occurred with Datadog's admission controller, when a default deny policy was applied and the network policy allowing ingress to Datadog's admission controller was miss...
items.answer:
Pod admission can fail due to webhooks + context deadline exceeded, even when all webhooks are set to failurePolicy = Ignore

### Anything else we need to know?

It seems that pod admission has a global 30 second timeout. By specifying 4 webhooks, each with a timeout of 10 seconds, it is possible to exceed that timeout and cause pod admission to fail, **even when all webhooks have failurePolicy set to Ignore**. This also results in a message that just says "context deadline exceeded", and doesn't name the offending webhooks, since they didn't actually cause the failure. This makes it super hard to debug, as you have to dig into the kube-apiserver looks to find the offending webhook. It also seems unintentional: my expectation was that having no webhooks set to `failurePolicy: Fail`, pod admission should not be able to fail due to webhooks.

We have to limit the time spent handling the request, so the failures of those webhooks _were_ ignored, but if they're collectively too slow then the handler will still fail.

items.question: What resolution or maintainer guidance was provided for issue #128684 (No overflow validation when using MilliValue())?
items.ideal_answer: > Since most calls to MilliValue() do not verify that the number is small enough first, we think the simplest fix might be let MilliValue() or ScaledValue() handle overflow automatically. For example, capping the return value at maxInt64 when overflow occurs.
items.answer:
No overflow validation when using MilliValue()

> Since most calls to MilliValue() do not verify that the number is small enough first, we think the simplest fix might be let MilliValue() or ScaledValue() handle overflow automatically. For example, capping the return value at maxInt64 when overflow occurs.

Or moving callers to a new method say `CheckedMilliValue() (int64, error)` that signals error/overflow, or auditing for our callers and having them actually check value first at the call site?

### What did you expect to happen?

Although it's unlikely that we will encounter these extremely large values in real world, there is no constraint on the range of this value. Therefore we expect no overflow happens regardless of the user's input.

1. Since most calls to `MilliValue()` do not verify that the number is small enough first, we think the simplest fix might be let `MilliValue()` or `ScaledValue()` handle overflow automatically. For example, capping the return value at maxInt64 when overflow occurs.

2. Another possible fix can be to add a range constraint of [MaxMilliValue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847be850000a902bcd82fb4a02bada5d948595a0/staging/src/k8
